content.content: Erbakan's accession

In contrast with how party affairs usually work, the MSP leadership has announced the conservative Süleyman Arif Emre’s resignation as the party chairman and Necmettin Erbakan’s, a mechanical engineer and the leading figure of the Islamist politics, designation as the leader. Erbakan’ ascension represents a victory for his unique vision of Islamism: a vision he calls the “National Vision”.

Since the MNP’s, the predecessor of the MSP, formation in 1970 there have been disagreements in the party over which principles should define the Islamic Conservative party, a political brand that hadn’t been adopted by any Turkish party until now. One camp advocated for continuing allegiance to the traditional right and desired the party to appeal simply to the right wing of AP. Another camp however, the one headed by Erbakan, wanted a complete break with the conventional right and for the establishment of a “Third Way” in politics, one that espouses National and Religious wellbeing against the dangers of both Communism and Capitalism.

The followers of the National Vision advocate for a dismantlement of excessive state institutions and their replacement with religious orders that would establish a degree of control over the lives of the citizens and thus be able to defend Islamic values. The movement also has a specific audience that we have found to be receptive to its messaging: the petty bourgeoisie. Even though the petty bourgeoisie already had conservative leanings before, as they are the local defendants of the political and economic order, they have recently found their true place in politics under the wings of Erbakan who promises them defence from “Capitalism” led by large corporations that came to crush many of them during Demirel’ tenure. Even though our views are irreconcilable, their economist interventionist stance paradoxically parallels ours.

As Erbakan rises over the top and establishes firm control over his party, it is best to remember how he came to be where he is today. Originally a mechanical engineer affiliated with the Süleyman ağa cult, he first entered politics in the aftermath of the 1960 coup. Even partaking in the discussions over the new economic agenda of the junta, he began advocating for a form of decentralized industrialization where local producers would unite to form larger factories which would provide the backbone of a new economy. Even though his ideas were rejected by the economics committee of the junta, he found a receptive audience among the local producers of Istanbul that he began to organize a cartel. The organization gradually spread across Anatolia and Erbakan had become a figure too big to ignore.

Such was the reason when in 1969 Demirel, sensing the threat of an insurgent anti-monopoly movement, got Erbakan thrown out of TOBB that he had just been elected as the chairman of. The relations between the two figures worsened over time in a series of disputes and this dynamic to a degree may be responsible for Erbakan’s staunch denouncement of attachment to the AP. Nevertheless, he is no longer the man to direct MSP from the shadows and has once again, dangerously for the right, “become too big to ignore”.

content.content: AP is the center right to right wing party that has been dominating Turkish politics for the last 10 years. Formed as a successor to the banned Democrat Party after the coup of 1960, AP quickly came to outgrow all the other self proclaimed successors to the 'Demirkırat', a vulgarized version of the word 'Democrat' created by the masses not used to the word, tradition of the Democrat Party and established itself as the primary party of the right.

Although AP is not an anti-republican party, similar to the Democrat Party, the party as a whole has opposed the democratization reforms implemented during and after 27 May. AP achieved significant electoral victories by appealing to the rural farming class and small business owners. However, once in power, AP's economic policies, similar to those of Democrat Party, favored the landowning elite and the industrial class. This shift increasingly alienated the party from its poorer rural and urban constituents. This alienation has weakened AP's electoral position, as its grassroots support has shifted to other right-wing parties. The establishment of DP has introduced a significant competitor for the average right-wing voter. Simultaneously, the small business class, previously neglected by AP, has found new representation in the Islamist MSP.

The leader of AP Süleyman Demirel is an interesting character. Born in 1925 to a family in rural Isparta, Demirel became a successful engineer and climbed the ladders of technical success. He began working in the general directorate of electrics in the early 50's, became a member of the leading council in 1953 and was appointed its leader by prime minister Adnan Menderes in 1955. After participating in politics for the first time by joining AP in 1962, he quickly rose within the party as well and was elected its leader in 1964. Serving as the prime minister between 1965 and 1971, his second term was cut short by the 12 March memorandum which began an era of military dictated governments which still continues today. However even though Demirel was the one whose government was forced into resignation by the military, both the military and the AP have been enthusiastic collaborators in governing the country since the military's memorandum on March 12th 1971.

Nowadays Demirel is associated with many adjectives: 'Barajlar Kralı' or 'The king of dams' by his followers due to his successes in development projects during the 1960's, 'Morrison' by his opponents in the party due to him briefly working for an American engineering company called Morrison and 'Çoban Sülü' or 'Shephard Süleyman' due to his agrarian upbringing. Demirel is generally associated with technocracy, accessibility and most importantly his ability to politically survive against all odds and circumstances. However his liberalism should not lead us to think of him as a harmless figure; Demirel is a master of survival and has shown in the last decade his willingness to cooperate with the far right if it means controlling the left.

content.content: Mustafa and his squad marched through the hills of the Five Finger Mountains. Their bags, rifles and boots were covered in the filth that they had to pass through while advancing along the Greek lines. On their shoulders they carried the weight of the 4.4 kilograms G3 rifle, 10 kilograms of infantry hardware and varying amounts of ammunition hanging from all over their bodies. However the most pressing weight of it all was the terror of realizing the fallacy of innocence and not knowing whether you will be alive tomorrow or not. So the young men kept marching through the steep hills and the rocky terrain, for that was the only way of not thinking about what they were going through.

By dawn the squad reached the village of Karaman as they were instructed. The village had been captured by the TMT already and they were instructed to establish a command post in the village. However, as men entered the village and marched through its dirt streets, they were appalled by what they saw.

In the middle of the village and surrounded by tens of Turkish villagers was a Greek young man tied up to a wooden chair and another Turkish man with an old pistol in his hand. Patches of redness covered the young man's clothes and the old man walked and swang his pistol frenzily and in a manner where the gun seemed both too heavy and unsuitable for his hand. He may have been holding a gun for the first time.

Mustafa walked through the crowd to see what had gathered the villagers so early in the morning. Just as he broke through the ring of the gossipping crowd, he saw the old man kick the young man in the groin and throw him to the ground. Another kick and blood sprayed across the ground like water color. Mustafa pulled his rifle and shouted:
"Leave him! What's happening?"
The old man raised his head and smiled. "Don't get involved, soldier. This is not your battle."
"Give up your pistol! Why are you doing this to him?"
"He is one of them."
"One of who?"
The old man shouted with a sense of mania and outburst. "The Greeks. They are going to pay for what they have done."

Mustafa felt his thumb trembling while pulling the rifle's hammer. "This is not why we are on the island. The enemy is not the common man but those who drive them against one another. What did he do to you?"

The old man looked him in the eye with a decaying excitement. He stopped for a moment before speaking up in a chalky voice. "His life is for retribution. Men from EOKA raped my only daughter and killed her in a bathtub. They made me watch her bleed to death."
As Mustafa felt the rifle falling from his hands, he heard a bang that he quickly turned his head against.
When he finally gathered himself enough to look, he saw the young man with a star shaped hole in his eye. And heard the screams of a hundred.

content.content: 15 July 1974

Immediately after news of the coup, the eyes of the whole world turned to Ankara. Messages began pouring into the Foreign Ministry by telegram, telephone and visits from ambassadors. Led by UN Secretary-General Waldheim and NATO Secretary-General Luns, Britain, America, France and all the allies repeated the scenario familiar from years past: "Please act calmly."
Ecevit concluded the discussions as follows:

"To invoke Article 4 of the Treaty of Guarantee, drawn up for the independence of Cyprus, and to change the Sampson regime, a Turkish military presence on the island is necessary. In this way, we can protect both Turkey's security and that of the Turkish Cypriots. Preparations must begin. Meanwhile, we shall also contact Britain, the other guarantor country, and try to achieve our objectives without bloodshed. If we obtain no result from Britain, we shall have completed our preparations to exercise our right in practice."

That night, Ecevit told his ministers that Greece could no longer be regarded as a guarantor country and that he would therefore hold talks with Britain. Even those who understood that intervention lay at the end of the road had countless questions. What would the Greek reaction be? What if a Turkish-Greek war broke out? And so on, and so on.

At around 2.30 in the morning, the ministers gave the prime minister "full authority". This authority covered conducting diplomatic contacts with Britain and other countries, as well as following the recommendations of the National Security Council.

content.content: 16 July 1974

He settled on the following strategy: he would call on Britain to activate the machinery of the Treaty of Guarantee, conduct the relevant contacts, go to London if necessary, and show that he had "tried every avenue".

At the end of the cabinet meeting, it was decided to approach Britain immediately. Since the British ambassador was then on his summer holiday, a note was handed to the counsellor, requesting a reply within twenty-four hours. The note formally requested "immediate talks to invoke the Treaty of Guarantee".

content.content: 17 July 1974

The prime minister made a fairly long speech. He said that if Sampson became established, no organization or country would be able to bring about a change in Cyprus, whereas such a situation would be unacceptable to Turkey and to the Turkish community there.
Wilson listened attentively. The prime minister made it clear that Turkey could not remain a spectator to the coup and put forward his proposal:

"If you do not want bloodshed and an irreparable wound in NATO, let us conduct the operation together. Agree to allow Turkish forces to use the British bases. If we enter the island from your bases, it will be bloodless. I am calling on you to fulfil your duty under the Treaty of Guarantee."
Wilson said they knew what sort of man Sampson was and shared their concerns:
"The opportunity to restore the old order has not yet been lost."

"Every passing hour makes matters a little more difficult. Sampson must be removed and a new order established in Cyprus. The balance has been completely upset. We are determined to secure the Turkish community's safety. For that, the Turks must be given an outlet to the sea..."
"Let us invite Greece too and hold a tripartite meeting here. Kissinger is continuing his efforts as well. The United Nations is meeting. There is no need for military action."
"The balance in Cyprus has been upset beyond restoration. This cannot be put right by platonic statements or resolutions. Greece is responsible for the coup and cannot be accepted as a party."
The talks continued. Wilson wanted to steer matters towards negotiations:
"We are in contact with Greece. We have asked for the replacement of the officers responsible for the coup and are awaiting a reply."
Ecevit was conciliatory and made no threats. As a diplomat at the meeting put it, he did not use grand declarations such as "if you do not do this, I shall go", as had happened in the past.

"We must think humanely. The present Sampson regime will change. If Turkey is forced to act, it will have to do so alone. Blood will be shed, whereas we could settle this by creating as little conflict as possible. The only way to do that is to use your bases."
This time Callaghan interjected:
"There will be war with Greece. Athens cannot stand by and watch. NATO will be shaken."
Having tried every avenue without obtaining a result, the British prime minister ended the talks:

"The status of the bases has been defined quite clearly... There is no possibility of sending Turkish troops out from them... Nor do we accept the view that the Treaty of Guarantee gives Britain the right to armed intervention."

options.title: Continue.

content.content: 18 July 1974

Immediately after Ecevit repeated what he had said to Wilson and Callaghan, Sisco took the floor and began speaking quite forcefully to dissuade Turkey. He had also brought a message from Kissinger to the same effect:
"America opposes a Turkish intervention because of the coup. We think this could lead to war between two NATO members."

After stating that Turkey had no intention of going to war with Greece, Ecevit tried to dispel the American administration's concerns. Beginning with the decision on poppy cultivation, he discussed Turkish-American relations and the periods through which they had passed. He even said that friendships could endure as long as they rested on sound and equal foundations. He said that even the Sixth Fleet could now visit Turkish ports more safely, because relations rested on a healthy foundation:
"...But it is impossible for Turkey to turn a blind eye to a fait accompli in Cyprus."

"But you are not considering Greece's reaction. They will not leave this unanswered. War will break out and the region will be thrown into turmoil. You should know that your relations with the United States will also deteriorate."
"That is for them to decide."

The end of the meeting with Sisco, which had been interrupted after lunch and resumed for half an hour in the afternoon, was very interesting. Sisco, known as Kissinger's closest associate, had spoken with Callaghan and returned to Ecevit. He persisted in his position and seemed to have realized that the danger of intervention was much greater than he had estimated. According to those who witnessed it, the following exchange took place:
"Mr. Ecevit, I am going from here to Athens. Give me your conditions in writing. We shall take them to the Greeks. I shall then return to Ankara and inform you of their answers."
Ecevit dictated them one by one:

"Our conditions are quite clear. To restore the balance and secure the Turkish community's safety, the presence of Turkish troops on the island must be accepted. Sampson must be replaced immediately, the Greek officers withdrawn, the Turkish community granted an area with an outlet to the sea, and a system established to control entry to and exit from the island. In other words, Turkey must be granted the opportunities the Greeks currently possess."
In a speech many described as "clear and resolute", Deniz Baykal explained the Ecevit government's "crisis diplomacy" (Realpolitik) and made it clear to the leaders that intervention was approaching.

"How does the government view events? In our view, the London and Zurich agreements had lost their validity even before the coup. They continued in practice. The Treaty of Guarantee was also losing its effectiveness, and Turkey was unable to protect its rights arising from the agreements. This is the underlying cause of the latest events. We must now do more than explain our rights; we must take matters further. We shall seek our rights on the basis of an independent Cyprus. Our first objective is to ensure that the Turkish community obtains at least one port. There is a movement in the world to bring Makarios back. But that is not our objective. If we act, paths beyond London and Zurich may open before us. We do not regard the latest developments as a simple coup..."

content.content: 19 July 1974
The Sisco-Ioannidis meeting was very heated.

"Ioannidis absolutely did not believe in a Turkish intervention. Despite all Sisco's efforts, he did not change his attitude. When he read the conditions sent by Ecevit, he became angry and said, 'They might as well have asked for Athens too; if they are so confident, let them make a landing.' He said that in such a case war would certainly break out and Greece would attack Turkey. These words probably had to be taken seriously. Ioannidis continually spoke of Makarios's immorality and his cooperation with the Russians. He said that Sampson's arrival had settled the Cyprus problem at its root. He was in a strange state of mind. He did not want to listen to anyone and told Sisco to stop the Turks, otherwise NATO would collapse."

Greece was not accepting the Turkish proposals. Tasca, the American ambassador in Athens, suggested to Kissinger that in these circumstances the Sixth Fleet must move between Cyprus and Turkey and prevent an intervention. There was no other way out. Kissinger's reply was categorical:
"NO. Do not become hysterical."
Foremost among the reasons was the possibility of the Soviet Union becoming involved. Moreover, this would amount to "a second Johnson letter" and the complete loss of Turkey.
Sisco began speaking like a businessman:

"I have spoken with the Greek authorities. There are important changes in their position. In particular, they agree to replace the officers involved in the coup. Moreover, after a certain transitional period, it appears possible that Sampson could be replaced by someone more moderate. They promise elections and have stated in particular that no harm will come to the Turks' safety. Sampson has also made statements to this effect. They guarantee that intercommunal talks will begin immediately."

An icy atmosphere swept through the room. Athens had rejected every point on which Turkey insisted: placing some important sea and air ports under joint administration, accepting the presence of Turkish forces there and providing them with entry and exit facilities like those of the Greeks, immediately changing the present regime, and granting the Turkish community an outlet to the sea. It was content with verbal guarantees alone.

content.content: 20 July 1974

"The Turkish Armed Forces' airborne and landing operation in Cyprus has begun. May God make it beneficial to our nation, to all Cypriots and to humanity. We believe that in this way we shall have rendered a great service to humanity and peace. I hope that our forces will not be fired upon and that there will be no bloody clash. We are going to the island not for war but for peace, to bring peace not only to the Turks but also to the Greeks. We reached this decision only after trying every political and diplomatic avenue and being compelled to do so. I consider it my duty to express my gratitude to all friendly countries, including our friends and allies the United States and Britain, with whom we have recently been in close consultation, for their well-intentioned efforts to settle the matter without intervention, through diplomatic means. If these efforts produced no result, the responsibility certainly does not lie with the states that made these well-intentioned efforts. Once again, I hope that this action will be beneficial to humanity, to our nation and to all Cypriots. I pray that God protects our nation and all humanity from disasters."

Sisco, who was in Athens at the time, was aware of this panic. He had been unable to stop Turkey, but he had at least to prevent a Turkish-Greek war. What Kissinger, and therefore America, categorically did not want, and was ready to use every threat to prevent, was war between two NATO members.

Turan Güneş opened the door and entered the prime minister's office, looking around. As he went out as though he had failed to find what he was looking for, he said to the person typing at the desk opposite, "Look, have you seen the prime minister?" and burst into laughter. Bülent Ecevit was at his typewriter, writing the speech he would make in parliament that afternoon.
"Mr. Bülent, Sisco has sent a message from Athens. He wants to come today. We have nothing left to say... I do not want to see him."
"The operation has begun now. I too think there is nothing to discuss."
Güneş asked his aides to inform the US embassy that, because the region was very dangerous, the General Staff was not granting landing permission for Sisco's aircraft.

The operation had begun only a few hours earlier, but telephone calls were pouring in from the most unexpected places: please cease fire! From the UN secretary-general's message and the NATO secretary-general's telephone call to French pressure at embassy level and German interventions, the Foreign Ministry and the prime minister's office hummed like a beehive with messages saying, "Please stop. War with Greece could break out."

content.content: The 'Güzel İstanbul' Affair

The contrast between Kemalism and Islamism isn't only in the political sphere but has connotations for social and artistic life as well. In the Islamic culture sculpture has long been shunned due to the hostility towards idolatry and paganism that each prophet was told to have fought against. In contrast, since the foundation of the republic the Kemalists have spent great efforts to import western arts including sculpture in order to break with the nation's Ottoman past.
Last week, on the 10th of March, some artists displayed the sculpture of a naked woman in the popular Yıldız Park in İstanbul, titled 'Güzel İstanbul' or 'Beautiful İstanbul'

Displaying a naked woman looking up towards the sky and bound by shackles on her wrists, the statue is intended to be a universal representation of the emancipation of women. However the conservative newspapers and news outlets have quickly begun attacking the statue for its nudity, with the Islamist Sabah newspaper saying it 'morally corrupted Muslim Turks' for its displaying of Female genitals.

The tensions quickly came to a head as a group entered the park in the midnight on the 18th of March. In a 'sledgehammer operation', the group assaulted the statue, broke it from its plinth and ripped its arm off, disposing it in a dumpster afterwards. While the statue is in a repairable state, the event has showcased the rising tensions between the two sides of the political aisle.

However the Demirel government seems to have bowed down to the whims of the fundamentalists to not anger their coalition partner MSP. Islamists claim victory as the statue is disposed in a construction site, far away from the public but close to the value AP apperantly attributes to the right of free expression.

content.content: İsmet İnönü looked out the window. It was getting late, as evidenced by the orange and red slowly replacing the blue over the horizon. As the sun started retreating away from eyeview, the rays of light it diffused over his bedroom also began shrinking more and more. As İnönü saw, he in his decripit rocking chair would be left in darkness in a few hours, with no one to save him.

İnönü wondered to himself, "when did it come to this?". He had spent years as the right-hand man of Atatürk, balancing the ambitious and energetic man with his cautiousness and mindfulness. He remembered the good old days when the republic was declared and the joy in the eyes of everyone who believed in a better future for the Turkish people than being the subjects of a reactionary monarch. He remembered the restless nights he spent during his time as the commander in chief of the Western Front during the War of IndependenceThe Turkish War of Independence took place between 1919 and 1923 after the Entente Powers attempted to impose the harsh Treaty of Sevres onto the Turkish nation.. Atatürk had built the nation and İnönü made sure it did not falter, as to both serve his duty for the nation he had devoted his life to and honor the legacy of his best friend.

But now he was being dumped by his own party! The party he had fostered with Kemal and led for more than 30 years! He was disappointed and angry, for he did not want things to be the way they are. Had he not done his best to not lose the spirit of his time? Had he not accepted and even pushed for the first free elections in 1950, put the party on the course of the Left of Center and accommodate Ecevit as general secretary for the sake of his energy? Hadn't he fought getting old enough? The thoughts swarmed his mind: once the defender of the progressive republic, now he was being thrown away like a relic of the past!

As he felt the rays of sunlight leave the vertex of his head, he turned his chair around and stared down the passing sun. It was beautiful. Not as straightforward as the daytime perhaps but blooming with colors of different shades, something not possible under sunlight. Perhaps that was what was needed for the republic. Even though his time may be over, perhaps the ideals he and Kemal espoused may live in another form; after all, what if his dusk was the dawn of someone else?

He thought of the alternatives. Ecevit? No. He was merely a social democrat interested more in mauling the Marxists than he was in solving the actual problems of the workers. He did not have the capacity of controlling over such a large party as such an undisciplined man. Perhaps what irritated him the most was that even though Kırıkoğlu had been the one who brought him into the party, it was not him but Ecevit who was led by destiny to lead the movement against İnönü.

content.content: Born from an affliction of the veneration of violence, the glorification of power and the paranoia of change, the MHP is the embodiment of reaction. It is a cult of authority where its followers only abide and respect brute force, and feel a barbarous desire to submit to the supreme leader, the Chieftain or the “Başbuğ”. This is the sentimentality that gave rise to the ultranationalist party known as the MHP, and today reminds us of the primitive face of humanity as the pinnacle of tribalism and primal instincts.

The 1960’s saw the rise of Socialist politics, both in the form of the electoral successes of TİP and the increased presence of Socialist ideals in the intelligentsia and mainstream politics. However, this shift also gave birth to a rabid reaction born out of the fear of radical change and the dismantling of social hierarchies. The party embodying this sentiment, MHP, was founded in 1969 through a renaming of the more moderate right wing nationalist CKMP. The revitalized party blended Turkish Nationalism and Islamism into a new form of nationalism known as the “Turkic-Islamic Synthesis” or “Idealism” which defined Turkicness along the lines of Islam and adherence to the conservative cultural norms. The party also boasts a paramilitary organization known as the “Grey Wolves” who strictly follow the fundamentalist party line and serve as the loyal lackeys who do the dirty work of assaulting and murdering the students and intellectuals who dare sympathize with Socialist ideals. Prior to the 12 March memorandum, tens of thousands of these so-called “commandos” had been trained in rural Anatolia by nationalist figures such as Muzaffer Özdağ and Alparslan Türkeş, ready to beat what they cant through words with bullets.

The leader of these men is Alparslan Türkeş, a self-proclaimed “strong-man” with the sole power to distinguish the right and wrong for his movement and the will to realize the dreams of an “uncorrupted” Turkey. Originally known as the Colonel who announced the 1960 coup against Adnan Menderes in the state radio, TRT, Türkeş had been part of the radical branch of the junta which opposed the reversal to democracy and desired the establishment of an authoritarian state. After the victory of the moderates in the junta, Türkeş was de-facto exiled to India and warded off from political power. However he returned to Turkey after the restrictions eased and got elected as the leader of CKMP in 1965, intent on transforming Turkish nationalism into a cult of authority and tradition. He used to pound the podiums with his sullen voice and proclaimed for the elimination of “foreign influences” which were corrupting the minds of the people, until the 12 March Memorandum put him and his party under scrutiny.

However, their recent silence should not relieve us, for it is a bandage for a wound that is still bleeding inside. Until the day our nation progresses enough to leave the nostalgia for the past and its traditions behind, Türkeş and his sycophants will keep proudly waving their banner of the three crescent, symbolizing “the three continents Turkicness dominated once: Europe, Africa and Asia"

However it would be erronous to think of this government as a truly stable cabinet to govern for an entire term; it is merely a stepping stone for both sides in pursuit of their political objectives, after which it would be thrown into the dustbin of history.

The Far Right Islamist MSP's willingness to form a government with us, the defenders of the republic and laicism, only came as an attempt for MSP to distinguish itself from AP and the moderate right. Warfare and bloodshed have been a constant norm in the politics of the Middle East for long, however this fact has been reiterated once again with the Yom Kippur War. Arabian armies, which initially held the advantage on the battlefield, have been utterly and decisively defeated by the Israeli army and the war has proven to be a decisive victory for the young Jewish State.

As the spilt blood began to dry under the heat of the sun, the Arabian states accused the Western Powers, especially the US, of orchestrating the Israeli victory and in a sudden announcement, OPEC has declared a general decrease in the oil production and a ban on the oil exports to the western nations.
The decision came after the American president Richard Nixon put forward a bill to supply Israel with 2.2 billion dollars in the congress against the invading Arabian armies.
Shortly after the embargo, the price of oil spiked from 2$/barrel to 5$/barrel and immediately hit hard the developed and developing nations, one of which is us.

Overnight the already vulnerable Turkish economy has been hit hard by the rise in the price of oil. With both the nation and the industry struggling, we have to find a solution as soon as possible, or else our government may end earlier than we would like it to.
As overnight the economy crumbles, we will see whether Demirel can cope with the crisis or not

content.content: The pilot watched as the motor stopped. He tried strangling the steering wheel, to fly upwards and away, but nothing in the cockpit moved. He looked out the glass window and saw the battlefield underneath, with the trenches, the anti air guns(one of which must have been the one who shot his motor), and the tanks crushing the fertile ground. He looked again, towards the horizon this time, and saw the great sea. The Mediterranean it was, scretching far into the unknown, after which safety lay with the homeland. He wanted to go there, see his children again, and escape the atrocity of sudden death. He choked the steering wheel and lifted it upwards with all his remaining might. Yet he was beaten as he felt the plane diving downwards.

He had feared death a lot, yet feared his fear of death being known ever more. He volunteered in the airforce, took the most unbelievable and stupid risks just to hide this fear. Yet as the end looked him in the eye now, he realized the futility of it all. He took out his wallet and looked at the picture of his children once more, for the last time.

As the plane warped through the clouds and the rocky ground became visible, the pilot began imagining. He wrapped the steering wheel and flew upwards. He passed through the clouds and left the fear of death and violence and bloodshed and many more fucking atrocities behind. He flew up through the blue sky that the redness behind the clouds could not penetrate. He flew, flew and flew and finally arrived at his imaginary homeland where there were no bombing campaigns, no anti air guns, no split families, no children left fatherless and where no young men were sent to die in preventable conflicts.

'The Raiders flew over the battlefields and crashed headfirst into the enemy formations. They, with their rapid cavalry and light weaponry, massacred the enemy and built hills out of the skulls of the men they butchered and ran over. They sow fear and confusion among the infidels facing the Sublime State and the crescent of Islam shined over each puddle of blood spilt on every battlefield.'

The raiders ceased to be a thing over 150 years ago, with them being replaced by the modern Ottoman army which unlike the raiders moved with strategy instead of frenzy and prioritized controlledness over fanaticism.

Yet, the memory of the forgotten Ottoman regiment is being revitalized at the hands of the MSP and the Islamist youth movements, being remanufactured and reimplemented to suit an era which has neither the need for such medieval troops nor their outdated tactics, but rather their fanaticism in order to foster a youth as devoted and as willing to die for the cause of Islam as the raiders originally were.

For years, since the coup of 1960 a battle has been waging between the reformists who wished to reposition CHP as a Social Democratic party and the old guard which hoped to stall or even prevent such a transformation that they saw as a betrayal of the values of Kemalism.
However, the resolution of this long-lasting conflict seems to be approaching.

With Ecevit's victory in his conflict with İnönü on the chairmanship, the Left of Center has emerged as the triumphant faction within the party. With the rapid transformation of the party and its executive, the Right Kemalists have chosen to abandon CHP and carve out a separate path to offer a 'national' alternative to the Social Democratic CHP appearing in the horizon.

Roughly 30 delegates, led by Kemal Satır first and foremost, have collectively handed over their resignation to Chairman Ecevit and are currently independents, though we expect them to reach an agreement with CGP and its leader Turhan Feyzioğlu to merge their political paths very soon.

content.content: The Reformation of TİP

TİP had used to be the powerhouse of the Socialist movement and had been the first Socialist mass party in Turkey ever. However the 12 March 1971 Memorandum12 March Memorandum was an ultimatum delivered by the military for Prime Minister Süleyman Demirel to resign as a result of the increasingly anarchic situation in the late 60's and the Leftist coup attempt on 9 March. had led to the banning of the party with only one figure legally allowed to reestablish it one day: Leninist academician Behice Boran who had been serving as the former chairman.

Now that the restrictions on the political parties have been loosened, Boran and her allies have moved to reestablish the former spearhead of the Left. However due to many reasons, many Socialists' hesitancy to join a party dominated by Marxist LeninistsMarxism-Leninism is a far left ideology that wishes to overthrow Capitalism through a revolution which would be led by a vanguard party of ideologically loyal members. Such a party would lead the way towards a world revolution after which Communism, a stateless, moneyless and classless society would be achieved as the final stage of human history., the radicalization of the far left after the memorandum towards militancy and perhaps our pivot to the left, Boran's announcement of the reestablishment on the 1st of May did not raise the expected sensation. In contrast, with the gradual establishment of rival groups, the Socialist left is increasingly marching towards fragmentation.

The chairman prior to Behice Boran, Mehmet Ali Aybar, is said to have accelerated his efforts to form an opponent Democratic SocialistDemocratic Socialism is a left-wing ideology that wishes to overthrow Capitalism and establish a Socialist economy through democratic means. party, "Socialist Revolution Party" or SDP.

TSİP, Socialist Workers Party of Turkey, is establishing itself as a party in favor of establishing Socialism through a conciliation with religious values and military interventions based on the writings of Dr. Hikmet KıvılcımlıHikmet Kıvılcımlı was a psychiatrist and Marxist ideologue who advocated for a reconciliation of Marxist and Islamic values..

The supporters of MDD, a thesis for a "two-tiered" Socialist revolution which would begin first with the coup of "determined" young officers and then completed with a bloodless workers' takeover, are seemingly conciliating around the "Labourers' Party of Turkey", TEP.
And the illegal TKP , Communist Party of Turkey, which has long been banned since 1920 is also making a return with infiltrations in many Socialist organizations and unions; most prominently DİSK.

However, none of these parties seem capable of consolidating the Left like TİP had done over a decade ago. While the Left is in a chaos, the relations we cultivated previously with the unorganized cadres of TİP still hold on and will now be seen as our relations with the Socialist Left.

content.content: A spectre used to haunt Anatolia just like it did across Europe a few decades prior, before it was exorcised by the army in the 12 March Memorandum. Workers' Party of Turkey, TİP, was formed in 1961 after the new liberal constitution lessened political restrictions and allowed for new forms of political expression to arise. The party, even though it was originally founded by non ideological cadres, evolved to represent a vision for Socialism uniquely suited to the circumstances surrounding Turkey and wholly committed to liberal democracy.

The party in spite of hostility across much of the political spectrum managed to score a victory in the 1965 elections and send 15 delegates to the TBMM out of the 450 total representatives. The party, despite its total committence to parliamentary democracy, shook the Turkish elites and bourgeoisie to their core and represented a new vision of progress and welfare for the downtrodden masses.

In terms of ideology, TİP was marked by close ties with the rising syndicates and represented a form of Democratic SocialismDemocratic Socialism is a left-wing ideology that wishes to overthrow Capitalism and establish a Socialist economy through democratic means. determined to break out of the political fringes. Differently from much of the other Socialist parties across Europe and the Middle East, the party regularly breached classical Socialist iconography. The party utilized visual instruments in colors such as blue and green and made use of symbols derived from Turkish culture in order to seek appeal in a population that was actively being indoctrinated to fear the stereotypicalized left.

TİP separated into two approaches when it came to party structure: the first was the Democratic SocialistsDemocratic Socialism is a left-wing ideology that wishes to overthrow Capitalism and establish a Socialist economy through democratic means., which had Mehmet Ali Aybar "the Smiling Socialist" as their leader, advocated for a mass party. The second group was the Marxist LeninistsMarxism-Leninism is a far left ideology that wishes to overthrow Capitalism through a revolution which would be led by a vanguard party of ideologically loyal members. Such a party would lead the way towards a world revolution after which Communism, a stateless, moneyless and classless society would be achieved as the final step in human history., headed by a diumvirate of Behice Boran and Sadun Aren, advocated for a vanguard party that would lead the proletariat to socialism. Although Aybar and the Aren-Boran group had initially cooperated in building TİP, relations deteriorated over Aybar’s leadership and the limits of the party’s electoral-parliamentary strategy between 1965 and 1969. After TİP’s heavy defeat in the 1969 election, Aybar resigned as chairman, and the Aren-Boran faction took control of the party in 1970.

Currently TİP is banned after the memorandum on 12 March 1971 and many of its members are imprisoned and undergoing reportedly horrible treatment. Even though the spectre haunting Anatolia has been exorcised, many on the left dream of one day reestablishing the mass party and having it lead a socialist united front committed to real change through democratic means. However Behice Boran holds the rights for party chairmanship due to her status as the leader prior to the ban, and many Socialists do not find resurrecting the fading ghost desirable if it means having the party controlled by the Leninists.
Negotiations ease the immediate dispute, but our policy disagreements remain.

options.title: Is this seriously how they plan to achieve Socialism?

content.content: TKP/ML is formed!

Marxism in Turkey is largely acceptive of the achievements of the Kemalist Revolution, which is viewed as a Bourgeoisie progressive revolution led by a benevolent figure and needs to be completed with a transformation into Socialism. One man within the Marxist community stayed away from this analysis, and this was İbrahim Kaypakkaya. Seeing Atatürk and his actions as tyrannical and oppressive despite its claims of being the representative of the Enlightenment, Kaypakkaya has long advocated for a Socialist movement that opposes the Kemalist establishment just as much it does with the reactionaries.
Kaypakkaya's dream might now come to reality.

With the void within Socialism militancy due to the annihilation of THKO led by Deniz Gezmiş and the weakening of THKP-C led by Mahir Çayan, both having a positive opinion of Atatürk and Kemalism, Kaypakkaya has moved on to fill in the void with his alike minded men and formed TKP/ML.

Endoring the Maoist doctrine of revolution from the countryside, many reports of Kaypakkaya and his bandits robbing caravans and trucks along the mountains and the plains have started coming to Ankara. While TKP/ML remains a minor organization for now, a lot depends on whether Kaypakkaya will be able to reorganize his group into a so called 'people's army' in the future.

The drums of war have begun beating once again in the heart of the Middle East. After the recent Sinai Crisis between Egypt and Israel and Israel's refusal to submit to the Arabic demands of total withdrawal, the Arabian states have striken rapidly and decisively against the young Jewish State once again.

The Egyptian and accompanying Syrian armies have been reported to have achieved several minor successes in the border towns and several skirmishes. While a crisis that we dont want to endulge ourselves in, it nevertheless has the potential to shake up the status quo across the whole region.
And the Middle East marches into war once again, making many commentators question whether permanent peace in the Levant is possible at all.

content.content: Ziverbey was a huge villa painted in white that stood menacingly in the heart of İstanbul. Originally built during the late Ottoman era as the residency of Zihni Pasha, now it is acting as a torturehouse under the eyes of the whole nation. But looking does not mean seeing, for the pains endured by these people go unnoticed while "life goes on" for the people who couldn't look at the consequence of their silence in the eye.

"I couldn't see anything since my eyes were tied. Some people had laid me onto the floor and taken my socks off. A device was placed onto my wrists. I felt a screw being jammed. Such a moment came that I wasn't able to move my legs. Oil, or some other kind of liquid, they applied to the base of my feet. Then the birch rod started hitting. At first, I thought I could bear the pain (...) but the pain of bastinade is like nothing else (...) one feels a pain that sinks up to the bones. At the beginning of it, I was holding myself to not scream. But then I let myself free, because no matter how much you try, you cant keep your voice in. First the growling begins, then it turns into a cry for help, and you turn into an animal. It has such a spiritual aspect that adds onto the physical pain. You see yourself as disgraced..."
- İlhan Selçuk, writer and intellectual

"Our interrogation technique was "special". Our men were special... An incorrigible communist alleged that she was raped with a truncheon. Pardon my saying so, but would our 20-21 year old stout boys need a truncheon? It defies all logic. As far as I know, the prisoners were merely slapped around."

content.content: 20 July 1974 — A foothold, not a front

As the 6th Marine Regiment held the road immediately behind the beach, the soldiers of the 50th Infantry Regiment began moving forward and organizing themselves. Scattered machine-gun fire started from the surrounding area, but it was not difficult to silence it. Landing thirty-one ships one after another on the tiny beach was no easy task. The fleet had already begun taking up positions for shore bombardment... Turkish jets were sweeping the areas around Kyrenia and Nicosia, but dropping far fewer bombs than expected. The order “Do not fire unless fired upon” was still in their ears... Two landing ships that had run aground were left where they were... Scattered fire was answered.
Mehmet Ali Birand, 30 Sıcak Gün, PDF page 135 — English translation of the source excerpt.

The Commando Brigade was increasingly making parachute landings in the area at Boğaz held by the Turkish Cypriot fighters. Although they encountered scattered gunfire, their landing and assembly were fairly easy. General Ersin, commanding them, used the fighters' radios to send “We have arrived safely” to Akıncı, the Commander of the Land Forces, in Adana. The following order came from Adana: “Join the forces landing from the sea without losing any time.”
Mehmet Ali Birand, 30 Sıcak Gün, PDF page 136 — English translation of the source excerpt.

Fire continued from the caves in the Beşparmak Mountains, and the pockets of resistance seemed endless.

content.content: 22 July 1974 — Before the ceasefire

In Cyprus, the pressure of the previous night had been relieved, but the Greek Cypriots were again becoming active after dark. The KYRENIA–GÖNYELİ–NICOSIA link had been established, however inadequately. Yet resistance continued inside Kyrenia, and fighting continued in the pockets in the Beşparmak Mountains. The airborne troops and those who had landed from the sea were about to join up. The General Staff was very pleased that the force, which had been fighting on the island for two days without reinforcements, had achieved this—in fact, this was the real success. The second-wave forces had set out on Sunday night, 21 July, and were about to reach the island. There were heavy tanks and armoured vehicles, and they would consolidate control over the area that had been captured.

content.content: 23 July 1974 — A ceasefire without security

In Turkey, Karamanlis's arrival, followed immediately by Sampson's overthrow and his replacement by Clerides, was met with mixed feelings. In every Turk's mind, Karamanlis was known as a man who had signed the London–Zurich agreements despite Makarios and believed in Turkish–Greek friendship... Clerides too had always inspired sympathy with his moderate and reasonable attitude. These two leaders' accession increased hopes that “the way to a solution in Cyprus would open”... In government circles, the boast “We have brought democracy to Greece” prevailed. A softer atmosphere had emerged... With Karamanlis's arrival, an entirely new and wide-ranging cooperation could be established between Turkey and Greece...
Mehmet Ali Birand, 30 Sıcak Gün, PDF page 255 — English translation of the source excerpt.

In Cyprus, however, the ceasefire existed only in words. Turkey was continually massing troops to make up the shortfall and trying to establish itself fully on the territory it held and ensure its security. The Beşparmak Mountains could not be cleared. Even in Kyrenia there was still resistance—contrary to what the newspapers were saying. The Turkish army was advancing little by little, both to silence the fire coming from the other side and to secure its own safety. The troops in Nicosia had also begun approaching the airport. From time to time, these expansions did go too far... The Turkish units were trying to make up the shortfall...
Mehmet Ali Birand, 30 Sıcak Gün, PDF page 255 — English translation of the source excerpt.

content.content: The 'Güzel İstanbul' Affair

The contrast between Kemalism and Islamism isn't only in the political sphere but has connotations for social and artistic life as well. In the Islamic culture sculpture has long been shunned due to the hostility towards idolatry and paganism that each prophet was told to have fought against. In contrast, since the foundation of the republic the Kemalists have spent great efforts to import western arts including sculpture in order to break with the nation's Ottoman past.
Last week, on the 10th of March, some artists displayed the sculpture of a naked woman in the popular Yıldız Park in İstanbul, titled 'Güzel İstanbul' or 'Beautiful İstanbul'

Displaying a naked woman looking up towards the sky and bound by shackles on her wrists, the statue is intended to be a universal representation of the emancipation of women. However the conservative newspapers and news outlets have quickly begun attacking the statue for its nudity, with the Islamist Sabah newspaper saying it 'morally corrupted Muslim Turks' for its displaying of Female genitals.

The tensions quickly came to a head as a group entered the park in the midnight on the 18th of March. In a 'sledgehammer operation', the group assaulted the statue, broke it from its plinth and ripped its arm off, disposing it in a dumpster afterwards. While the statue is in a repairable state, the event has showcased the rising tensions between the two sides of the political aisle.

Ministers from MSP and vice-prime minister Erbakan have called for the removal of the statue while intellectuals pressure the party to not bow to the whims of the Islamists and defend the right of artistic expression. Many in the party are also in favor of preserving the statue.

content.content: Lockout Wave in Bursa

Eight car factories in the industrial city of Bursa have enacted lockouts and prevented their workers from entering after a dispute between METAL-İŞ, a syndicate under the right wing TÜRK-İŞ, and the Turkish branch of the car manufacturer Renault.

The dispute arose after a disagreement over the terms of collective bargaining over the salaries of the workers. What began as a worker strike evolved into a total lockout as the major car manufacturers in Bursa such as TOFAŞ and Renault closed down their factories to force the workers into surrendering. Overnight over 5,400 workers were left without any income.

After the negotiations on weekend failed to bring any results, the TÜRK-İŞ executive blatantly threatened the companies with a logistically improbable general strike which also failed to achieve any meaningful result. Many including the DİSK, the leftist syndicate, officials we have contacted also think the lockouts may have been a move by the employers to ease the price restrictions for cars set by the government.

Even though eventually a watered-down deal was reached after MADEN-İŞ accepted slight salary improvements, the lockouts in Bursa are only the latest examples of a rising trend in the number of employee and employer conflicts. Strikes in cities such as İzmir, Eskişehir and Ankara continue to put strain on the economic wellbeing of our labourers. Even though Chairman Ecevit has already supported the locked out workers verbally, we can promise to pass a reform on restricting unlawful lockout if we come to government after the next general elections. content.content: Poppy Harvestation Ban

Poppy plants had always had a special place in Islamic culture due to the relaxative properties of the glue that is released when the plant is cut open. Indeed, poppy glue can be a moderately potent depressant when chewed and it has been used for that purpose for ages, even being rumoured to have been utilized by the Order of Assassins in the 12th Century to calm down their operatives.

Yet, with the invention of modern distillation methods a far darker side of poppy has been discovered. The plant can be used to produce the extremely dangerous drug heroin and Turkish opium is currently said to be flooding the Western markets: specifically, the US's one.

'Anatolian Dawn' is a text-based political simulator about a significant period marked by political instability and violence in Turkish history, the 1970's. Just like in the original 'Social Democracy, An Alternate History' game that this simulator is based on, the game moves forward through turns that last for two weeks and the turns progress with cards that can be selected from the various decks that one will encounter through their playtime. As the turns progress, the players will encounter events that they will have to maneuver through. Designed to be a both complex and enjoyable simulation of the 1970's, various mechanics and features the players will get to experience are displayed down below.
To start off, on the left side of the screen, one will encounter various tabs that will display information about the political, social and economic situation of the nation.

The 'Main' tab is the basic one that shows the rough outline of the general situation within the country, such as the date, who is the president, who is the prime minister and so on. One crucial value shown in this tab is the attitude of TSK(acronym for the Turkish Armed Forces) towards the general status of the nation and their belief in the democratic framework. The head of the general staff is crucial in the sense that even though they cant prevent or conduct coups on their own, they can determine the nature of a coup done by the military hierarchy, for an example if a coup only has the purpose of resetting the political status or to reshape the democratic mechanisms as a whole. In that sense even though they are supposed to not take part in the political matters, the head of the armed forces can influence the future of the nation greatly. Turkey's 1970's in real life ended with a bloody coup in 1980 and such a scenario may repeat itself if the army loses belief in the ability of the current system to effectively rule the nation, and if the root causes that carried the nation to such a terrible outcome aren't resolved. Thats where you, the player need to take action and both prevent the nation from following such a path and remove the systematic issues that would carry the nation towards that path in the first place.

The 'Politics' tab shows the general political situation in the nation. The key parameters displayed here are the inter-party relations which affect all aspects of the game, the party leaderships which display the ideologies that direct the decisions and attitudes of the various political parties, Kurdish nationalism which shows both how widespread Kurdish nationalism is among the Kurdish population and how violent it is against the state framework, union relations which shows how close our ties are with the labour movement and what whether left wing(DİSK) or right wing(TÜRK-İŞ) syndicates are more influential, municipalities control which shows how many provinces are governed by our mayors and the intra-party cliques within the party. All of these parameters need to be observed and managed carefully.

The 'Defense' tab shows the status of the paramilitary organizations that hold influence over the streets and the level of political violence, decided upon by the percentage of the state control over the streets compared to those of the far right and the far left groups. The objective of the player is not to empower either the far right or the far left but to resolve the political violence that if unsolved may be a huge milestone towards a military intervention. The police forces aren't immune to politics neither and their loyalty to the parliamentary and republican framework will need to be kept in check. If the street fightings become unmanagable, it will damage both our party and the rest of the parliamentary framework greatly and may prevent many of our political capabilities. This tab also shows the strength of the three branches of the armed forces, land, sea and the air which has the potential to influence the outcome of many of the inter-national situations that the nation will face throughout the 1970's.

The 'Polls' tab shows the vote percentage of the various parties around the nation and how popular they are in specific demographics. The National Kurdish Movement has the potential to spread and increase its demographic percentage if Kurdish Nationalism manages to reach a breakthrough among the previously politically inactive Kurds.
The 'Exterior Affairs' tab shows the international relations of our nation and the status of the various diplomatic crises that the nation will encounter.

The 'Economics' tab is one of the most striking points of the game and presents a complex economic simulation that will need to be managed by the players. The general health of the economy is a parameter affected by the other variables that affects everything ranging from party popularity to political violence. The Turkish economy is very vulnerable to the possible turbulances in the world economy and the fundamental issues that cause this weakness need to be resolved before another crisis hits and wracks the nation like a train.

Advisors are the influential politicians aligned with the party that take part in its governance and are able to take unique actions that varies from advisor to advisor. With actions being able to be taken one in specific periods of time, the players need to make the best of the actions that their advisors can provide, and create the suitable combination that will help them forward their cause and the party.

The Kemalist Revolution, which was guided by the founding father of the republic Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, was essentially an attempt to save the Turkish Nation from certain destruction at the hands of the Western Powers and their so called "servants" within the empire through rapid westernization and the adopting of modern republican values to keep up with the necessities of the Modern Age. The Turkish Republic, as was aforementioned, is a parliamentary democracy with a largely ceremonial president and a powerful prime minister and parliament called TBMM or the Turkish Great National Council. TBMM is responsible for passing legislation while the prime minister is responsible for handling the usual affairs of the state. The Prime Minister is elected by the parliament in accordance with the share of seats each party gets in a general election which is approximately proportional with its vote share. To be elected prime minister one needs a majority in the parliament which opens doors to possible coalition arrangements. The ability to form governments and become prime minister is given by the president, however unless there is a case of military coup the party with the most seats is usually given the upper hand.

The president is too elected by the parliament, however as the president is viewed to be a non-partisan and neutral position which sets out to unite all of the nation under its wings, usually technocrats or nonpartisan politicians are elected to the post by the parliament with a consensus of the parliamentary parties.

Turkey has had a troubled past with its military and the military looms over the politics of the young republic as the so called "defenders of the republic". However it is debatable how much of this is actually true and how much of the military oversight over politics is rooted in personal gain.

content.content: Presidential Election of 1973
The 7 year term of president Cevdet Sunay is finally coming to a close and now a new obvious question that is arising is, who is going to replace him?

In the election where both the upper chamber, Senate and the lower chamber, TBMM will participate, a majority of 318 out of the 635 total members is needed to elect the new president; which none of the camps below were able to reach as of yet.

From the military camp the now resigned commander of the armed forces Faruk Gürler seems to be the overwhelming choice. One of the names who rejected cooperation with the Socialist putchers in the 9 March attempt, Faruk Gürler has been able to gather the support of the other generals and the military behind his back. Though some within our party had chosen to vote for him in the former rounds, he consistently seems unable to get more than a third of the votes. There are rumours that in case Gürler is unable to be elected, the armed forces may begin a second intervention which may signal the death of the Turkish Democracy.

AP, with their huge parliamentary presence has stood behind Tekin Arıburun. Also a former soldier with known right leaning tendencies, he has been unable to gather a comfortable majority as some within AP have repeatedly rejected voting for him and many chose to vote for the DP candidate, Ferruh Bozbeyli.

The only candidate with a civil background, Ferruh Bozbeyli has repeatedly stolen 40-50 votes from Tekin Arıburun and prevented him from being elected. While normally a civil candidate would be our choice as well, Bozbeyli is a staunch conservative.

Our investigations reveal infuriating cases of cooperation with right wing groups in persecuting Kurds and Alevis. As the state finally begins taking action against such atrocities, these groups are thankful towards both our party and the democratic system.

We will be able to retake this action without a budget decrease in the future.
The libraries we are building have already started attracting lots of students.
